slides.title: JTA Trader — an automated trading system that only trusts what it can prove
bullets: An automated trading system that only trusts what it can prove
What it is · how it works · how it keeps improving · where it goes next
Project walkthrough · 2026-11-17
slides.notes: Welcome. This deck walks through the whole project for someone smart who does not trade for a living. The main section is plain language; the appendix has the technical detail. Every number is either MEASURED (read straight from a file or a backtest result) or ESTIMATED (rests on an assumption), and the tag on the slide says which.

slides.title: The one-minute version
bullets: It trades by itself — Many small, rule-based strategies run around the clock on crypto, US exchange-traded funds and futures. Each trade has a stop-loss and a profit target from the moment it opens.

It proves before it risks — A strategy reaches real money only after a historical test, charged with realistic trading costs, clears a pass mark that was written down before the test was run. Then it goes straight to real money.
It keeps learning — Failures go back into research, not the bin. AI agent sessions run the research, the reviews and the bookkeeping. A human operator sets strategy and risk policy.
slides.notes: Three sentences to remember. It trades automatically. It tests ideas on history, with full costs, before risking money. And it keeps learning, because every trade and every test feeds the next round of research. The rest of the deck explains each of these.

slides.title: How to read the numbers in this deck
bullets: R = one unit of risk — Before a trade opens, it gets a stop-loss. The money lost if the stop is hit is 1R. A trade that makes +2R made twice what it risked. One that hits its stop is −1R. R lets us compare strategies of any size without quoting money.

Expectancy — The average R per trade. +0.20R means that, on average, each trade earned a fifth of what it risked, after costs. Small positive expectancy, repeated over many trades, is what an edge looks like.

The two tags — MEASURED: read straight from a backtest result or a config file. ESTIMATED: depends on an assumption (e.g. an allowance for slippage). If we could not verify a number, it is not in the deck.
slides.notes: Two ideas make every later slide readable. First, R. We never quote money; we quote how many units of risk a trade made or lost. Second, the tags. A MEASURED number was read directly from a result file. An ESTIMATED number depends on an assumption, for example how much worse than expected our fills are.

slides.title: The problem: most trading ideas do not survive contact with costs
bullets: An idea that looks profitable on a chart is often an illusion. Three things usually kill it:
– Costs: exchange fees, slippage (getting a worse price than expected) and funding charges.
– Overfitting: rules tuned so tightly to the past that they describe noise, not a pattern.
– Moving the goalposts: deciding what counts as success after seeing the result.
Running a live book well is also hard: positions must be protected 24/7, and every close must be explained.
JTA Trader's answer is to make discipline mechanical: the rules are code and records, not willpower.
slides.notes: This is the core problem the project is built around. Lots of ideas look good on a chart. Most of them stop working once you charge fees and slippage, or once you test on data the idea was not tuned on. People also fool themselves: they pick the pass mark after seeing the result. The system is designed to make those mistakes hard to make.

slides.title: What JTA Trader is
bullets: 62 strategy legs — A leg is one strategy on one market and timeframe, e.g. “Ether trend breakout on 4-hour bars”.
14 accounts — 11 switched on to send orders, 3 in dry run (they log what they would do, but send nothing).
3 kinds of book — Paper (simulated money at the broker), real money, and prop-firm evaluation accounts (the firm's capital, the firm's rules).
Always on — Runs 24/7 on cloud servers. It never switches itself off; problems are handled trade by trade.
slides.notes: Concrete shape. The counts here were re-read from the configuration files on the day this deck was built (2026-11-17, repo commit d66f12260). 62 strategy legs are configured; 14 trading accounts are configured, 11 of them switched to send orders. Paper accounts trade with simulated money at the broker; real-money accounts trade the operator's capital; prop-firm accounts trade a firm's capital under the firm's rules.

bullets: Crypto — Bitcoin, Ether, Solana, XRP, Cardano, Avalanche and others, as perpetual futures on Bybit. Paper, real-money and mirror accounts. 5 legs trade real money here.
US funds (ETFs) — Broad index, bond, gold, silver and leveraged funds on Alpaca. Paper, real money, mirror and an options paper account. 4 legs trade real money here.
Futures — Micro index and metals futures on Interactive Brokers, on paper. A real-money account exists in dry run with no strategies yet.
Prop firms — 4 prop-firm accounts are configured; 3 are switched on. They must clear a stricter bar than real money.

slides.title: The strategy families, in plain words
bullets: Trend breakouts — Buy when price breaks above its recent range, sell when it breaks below. Catches big moves; loses small often.
Pullbacks — In an established trend, wait for a dip, then enter in the trend's direction.
Short-term scalps — Quick trades on 5- and 15-minute bars around specific price patterns.
Volatility & fades — Trade the break-out after a quiet squeeze, or bet a false break-out reverses.
Pairs & macro — Trade two related coins against each other; a slower, thesis-driven sleeve built from valuation and economic events.
Machine learning & AI desk — A learned model that picks entries; an AI trading desk that reviews open trades and proposes changes.
slides.notes: No single clever trick. A portfolio of simple, well-understood rule families, each tested separately on each market. The point is breadth plus honest testing, not secrecy.

slides.title: The life of a trade
bullets: 1. Data — Prices arrive from each broker connection, every bar, every market.
2. Signal — Each strategy checks its own rules on its own markets.
3. Risk check — Per-account limits decide yes/no and the size, in R.
4. Order — Sent with a stop-loss and a profit target already attached.
5. Manage — Brackets can move, but only on evidence.
6. Close & grade — Exit reason recorded; trade graded and fed back to research.
slides.notes: Every trade follows the same path. Market data arrives. Strategies check their rules. If a rule fires, the risk manager decides whether this account may take it and how big it is. The order goes out with a stop and a target already attached. While it is open, management may move the brackets. When it closes, the reason is recorded and the trade is graded.

slides.title: Every trade carries a real stop and a real target
bullets: Stop-loss from the start — Every order rests at the broker with a protective stop. That stop defines 1R.
A real profit target — The target is a prediction, not a placeholder. A target set so far away it can never fill counts as no target, and a checker flags it.
Real money today — Target at entry: 8 of 9 routings. Target revised in the trade: 1 of 9. Closing this gap is on the roadmap.
slides.notes: A rule the operator set: no fictional take-profits. Many systems put a target so far away it never triggers, which is a way of not having one. Here, each strategy's target must be a real prediction of where price is going, and the prediction should keep moving with the trade. A script measures compliance on every routing of a strategy to an account. Honest status: on real money, 8 of 9 routings set a real target at entry, but only 1 of 9 also revise it during the trade. That gap is open work, and the checker only lets the list of exceptions shrink.

slides.title: Active management: either bracket can move, on market evidence
bullets: The whole bracket — Stop: tighten, widen or move to a structure level. Target: extend, pull in or re-estimate. Position: partial or full close. Or hold, which is recorded too.
Market-triggered — Structure, volatility, momentum, regime, scheduled events or liquidity levels. Never P&L alone; never the clock alone.

Applied, then graded — Reviewed actions are applied through each account's own risk checks, with a ping per change. Each action class is graded on its own rule: a small cost for a material cut in risk, holding across time and beating chance.
slides.notes: Once a trade is open, the system may move the stop or the target, or close part or all of the position. The trigger must be something in the live market: structure, volatility, momentum, regime, a scheduled event. Never the trade's profit alone and never the clock alone. Both brackets always stay in place. Since 14 November, every action a reviewed recommendation names is applied through each account's own risk manager, and the operator gets a ping for each change. Each kind of action is still graded separately against a risk-adjusted, cost-aware rule.

slides.title: Risk controls that never switch the system off
bullets: Sizing in R — Each account risks a fixed fraction per trade, so one loss is always a known, small amount.
Two switches only — Account: live or dry run. Strategy: live or shadow. There is no hidden third switch.
Daily drawdown brake — Per account, when armed: past a day's loss limit, open trades stay protected and new ones are blocked until the reset.
Never self-halts — Failures are contained to the one trade or job and retried; persistent problems raise a flag to the operator while the system keeps going.
slides.notes: Risk is handled per trade, not by switching the whole system off. There are exactly two switches that decide whether something trades: one per account, one per strategy. The one sanctioned brake is a daily drawdown switch per account: once a day's loss reaches a set level, existing positions keep their stops and targets but no new trades open until the reset.

slides.title: Backtesting, explained simply
bullets: 1. Replay history — Run the exact rule over past prices, trade by trade.
2. Charge full costs — Fees, plus allowances for slippage and funding.
3. Test out of sample — Score it on time periods it was not tuned on, split into folds.
4. Pass mark first — The rule for passing is registered before the run, never after.
slides.notes: A backtest replays history and asks: if we had followed this rule, what would have happened? The trap is that you can always find a rule that worked in the past. So three protections: charge the full cost of trading; judge only on data the rule was not tuned on, split into several separate time periods called folds; and write down the pass mark before running the test.
slides.footnote: The current pass mark for most legs: out-of-sample net R, after the full cost stack, must be above zero (rule RULE-D1-STAGE0-NET-OF-FULL-COST, registered 2026-09-22).

slides.title: The promotion ladder: a backtest pass goes straight to real money
bullets: STAGE 0 · Backtest — Is there an edge, net of all costs?. Passes only by clearing a pass mark registered before the run, on held-out data.
STAGE 2 · Real money — Live, with a paper mirror. Entered directly on a Stage-0 pass. The mirror net-negative after costs → demoted.
STAGE 1 · Demo floor — Paper trading, for data. Home of every testing leg, and of demoted legs while they are iterated on.
slides.notes: This is how an idea becomes a real-money strategy. Stage 0 decides whether there is an edge, offline, on history, net of the full cost stack. Since 12 November there is no step in between: a strategy that passes Stage 0 goes straight to real money, with a paper mirror that copies it exactly. The first live trades are watched as a mechanical check, never as a gate. The demo floor, Stage 1, is where every strategy that has not passed yet trades on paper to generate data, and where a demoted strategy goes back to keep generating data while it is improved. If the mirror turns net-negative after costs over its window, the strategy is demoted to the floor.
slides.footnote: No soak step between a backtest pass and real money (operator, 2026-11-12). A paper or live record never proves an edge; it checks mechanics and cost.

slides.title: What “pass” means for real money
bullets: Held-out data decides — The chosen configuration must pass its pre-registered rule on data it was not tuned on, after fees, slippage and funding.
A committed record — The result is written by a script into an evidence record in the repository. A claim in a message is not a record.
Probation, not a block — The deflated Sharpe ratio is reported on every decision. A live strategy below 0.95 stays live but keeps iterating toward a version that clears it.
slides.notes: Two clarifications on the pass mark. First, real money is governed by a held-out test: the chosen configuration must clear its registered rule on data it never saw during tuning, net of the full cost stack, written into a committed evidence record. Second, a stricter statistic, the deflated Sharpe ratio, which corrects for how many variants were tried, is reported on every promotion but does not block it. A live strategy below its bar is on probation: it keeps an open research unit whose goal is a version that clears it.

slides.title: Three statuses, derived from the books
slides.notes: Every leg has exactly one of three statuses, and the status is computed from which accounts it is on, never typed in by hand. Testing legs trade on paper so even weak ideas generate data. Production legs trade real money plus the mirror. Inactive legs were retired by a written research record that also says what evidence would bring them back. Counts as of 2026-11-17.

slides.title: Prop-firm accounts clear a stricter bar
bullets: A prop firm funds a trader on condition they stay within daily and total loss limits.
A prop leg must clear the real-money bar PLUS a survival and expected-value test against the firm's own drawdown rules.
Prop trades are executed and protected automatically, like any other account.
4 prop accounts are configured; 3 are switched on to send orders.
slides.notes: Prop firms lend capital under strict drawdown limits; break them and the account is gone. So a strategy must clear everything a real-money strategy clears, plus a survival test against that firm's specific limits. Never a lower bar.

slides.title: Values: no fossil fuels on real money
bullets: What is excluded — 50 oil, gas, coal and energy-infrastructure funds and producers, long, inverse and leveraged.
Where it applies — Real money, prop accounts and the real-money mirrors. Paper accounts are exempt, so research keeps its data.
How it is held — One list in configuration, read by an automated test that fails any change re-opening a gap. A good backtest does not override it.
slides.notes: A values rule, not a performance rule. The operator asked on 17 November: “In general, I ask that we not trade fossil fuels.” Oil, gas, coal and energy-infrastructure funds are excluded from every real-money, prop and real-money-mirror roster. Paper accounts may still trade them, because the data helps research. No backtest result can re-open the list, and an automated test fails any change that would put one back on real money.
slides.footnote: MEASURED: config/values_exclusions.yaml; enforced by tests/test_values_exclusions_real_money.py. The quote is on record verbatim in that file.

slides.title: Costs are charged in full, and they matter
bullets: Fees — Each venue's trading fee is charged on every entry and exit in the backtest.
Slippage — An allowance of 3–5 basis points per round trip for getting a worse price than the chart shows. ESTIMATED.
Funding — Crypto perpetual futures pay or charge a periodic funding rate; the backtest charges an allowance for it. ESTIMATED.
The effect — On the 7 production legs with a fee-only figure, slippage + funding cut 2%–51% of net R. ESTIMATED.
slides.notes: Why we insist on the full cost stack. Taking the production legs that have a fee-only number on file (n = 7 of 9 production legs), adding slippage and funding allowances removed between 2% and 51% of their fee-only net result. That range is ESTIMATED because the slippage allowance is an assumption, not a measurement of our fills. A strategy that only passes on fees alone does not pass.

slides.title: The research loop: decide before you measure
bullets: 1. Ask — One question, with its data, its test and its decision rule written first.
2. Run — A dispatcher runs queued questions automatically on cloud runners.
3. Grade — The result is graded against the rule that was registered.
4. Act — Pass → next stage. Fail → back to research with a diagnosis.
slides.notes: Research is run as a queue of questions. Each question is written down with its data, its test and its decision rule before it runs, so the result IS the decision and nobody argues about it afterwards. The queue currently holds 2271 questions: 1908 done, 277 waiting, 71 retired, plus 124 parked as blocked.
slides.footnote: MEASURED: research/queue/*.yaml status fields — 2271 units: 1908 done, 277 queued, 71 retired; 124 more in research/queue/blocked/. Commit d66f12260.

slides.title: Iterate on levers, not on luck
bullets: Every strategy, ML model and live-trade action class goes through the same research workflow.
The centre of it is understanding how each lever moves the outcome, not pass/fail alone.
– Levers include entry timing, stop distance, target placement, market regime and timeframe.
A failed test returns with a diagnosis and the next lever to test.
Retirement needs evidence that no lever helps, plus a written test that would bring it back.
Weekly programme reviews check that every non-passing strategy has a live next step.
slides.notes: A rule the operator set on 1 November: when something fails, we do not just try a different random idea. We work out why it failed, identify the levers that could change the outcome, and test them one by one. A strategy is retired only when the levers are exhausted, never after a fixed number of attempts. The same applies to ML models and to the live-trade review.

slides.title: Live books check mechanics and cost, never edge
bullets: Mechanics — Did the signal fire, the order go out at the right size, the brackets rest at the broker, and the close get a real reason?
Cost — Are real fees and slippage in line with the backtest's allowances?
Demotion signal — The paper mirror's net-of-cost result over its declared window triggers demotion back to the demo floor.
Probation — A live strategy whose deflated Sharpe ratio is below its bar keeps an open research unit to build a stronger version.
slides.notes: Live and paper trades are watched closely, but they do not decide whether a strategy has an edge; a handful of live trades is far too few. They check that the machinery works and that costs match what the backtest assumed. The paper mirror of each real-money book is the early warning: if it goes net-negative after costs over its window, the strategy moves back to the demo floor, where it keeps trading on paper for data while it is improved.

slides.title: The trading desk and the live-trade review
bullets: Live-trade review — Every open package, every account. Mechanics first, then the best decision now, each option priced from the strategy's own history. 789 reviews on record.
Applied, with a ping — Recommended actions are applied through each account's own risk manager, with one ping per change. Each action class is graded afterwards.
The trading desk — An AI trader that enters, manages and exits its own trades. Today it trades on the demo floor only; real money is gated behind its own evidence.
Teaching the models — The desk's decisions become labels for the system's own models, which aim to take over the job.
slides.notes: Two AI functions work on live trades. The live-trade review looks at every open order package, checks the mechanics first, then asks what the best decision is right now. Each option, such as hold, tighten or close, is priced from that strategy's own backtest history, and one recommendation per package is written to an append-only record. Since 14 November, recommended actions are applied automatically under one standing mandate, through each account's own risk checks, with a ping to the operator. The trading desk is the other half: an AI trader that finds trades the strategies are not taking, today on the demo floor only. The system's own models learn from its decisions, with the aim of eventually replacing it.
slides.footnote: MEASURED: comms/live_review/reviews.jsonl, one line per review, all accounts, commit d66f12260.

slides.title: Run by AI agents, governed by a human
bullets: Manager + lanes — One manager session keeps the work register and dispatches narrow lanes, each with one question and a spending ceiling.
Mandates — 23 standing grants let evidence-backed decisions proceed without asking. Agents can propose; only the operator grants.
Daily sync — One brief a day: what came due, what was decided under mandate, decisions for the operator, what moved, what is running, spend.
Permission tiers — Docs and tooling: autonomous. Runtime changes: one OK. Strategy and risk: operator approval, or a committed evidence record.
slides.notes: Day-to-day operations are done by AI agent sessions. A manager session keeps one register of work and dispatches focused lanes, like the one that built this deck. The operator sets strategy and risk policy and grants standing authorizations, called mandates, for decisions the data can settle. Currently 23 mandates are granted and 1 is proposed. Agents may propose a mandate; only the operator grants one.
slides.footnote: MEASURED: config/mandates.yaml, commit d66f12260.

slides.title: Numbers you can trust
bullets: Provenance labels — Every number is MEASURED, ESTIMATED, FABRICATED or UNVERIFIED, and the four are never mixed.
“0” vs “could not look” — A count that reads zero must say whether we actually looked. Missing data shows as “—”.
Merged ≠ deployed ≠ observed — A change is only done when its effect is seen on the running system, and reports say which of the three is true.
Automated guards — Checks on every change keep rules, configuration and docs from drifting apart, e.g. a guard refuses a strategy on both paper and real money.
slides.notes: Small rules that stop the most common reporting mistakes. Every number carries a label saying whether it was measured or estimated, or worse. A zero is never allowed to hide the fact that we could not look. A missing value shows as a dash, never as zero. And automated checks run on every change to keep the documents, the configuration and the code in agreement.

slides.title: Machine learning today
bullets: ML entry model (5 crypto coins, hourly): +0.037R per trade over 907 held-out trades (2025-10 → 2026-09), net of costs.
ML entry model (US funds pool, hourly): +0.492R per trade over 207 held-out trades (2025-07 → 2026-10), net of costs.
Same ladder as strategies: offline evidence → in use; demotion → shadow, still scoring for data.
An inventory on 2026-11-11 counted 106 registered models; it proposed keeping 15, reviewing 19 and retiring 72 that nothing uses.
Lesson recorded: models fed only price data did not predict direction; the limit is labelled outcomes.
slides.notes: Where ML stands, honestly. Two learned entry models now trade real money: one on crypto and one on a pool of US funds. Each was promoted on a held-out window scored once, net of the full cost stack. Models follow the same flow as strategies: offline evidence goes straight to use, and a demoted model drops back to shadow, where it keeps scoring for data while it is improved. Earlier attempts to predict direction from price data alone failed offline; the lesson recorded was that the binding constraint is labelled outcomes, not computing power.

slides.title: The ML programme: ten decisions, one model family each
slides.notes: The ML plan cuts the life of a trade into ten decisions, from which markets to trade to grading a closed trade. Each decision is owned by exactly one model family, with one question, a baseline it must beat net of cost, a label, and an offline test. Each slot runs its own champion and challenger loop: the model in use is the champion, a retrained or new model is the challenger, and the challenger replaces it only by beating it on the same data and the same costs. Several slots have no model yet; they run on rules today, which is stated rather than hidden.

slides.title: Roadmap 1 — scale the real-money strategies
bullets: Active management as standard — Evidence-backed stop and target moves on every real-money strategy, and targets revised during every trade.
A mechanical ladder — Backtest pass → real money; mirror net-negative → back to the demo floor. Decided by registered rules and standing mandates.
More legs through Stage 0 — 50 testing legs keep iterating on their levers; each one that passes goes to real money.
New horizons — Daily and weekly holds, and sub-hour breakout families, tested net of cost.
slides.notes: Goal one on the roadmap is real-money edge, decided offline. The near-term work: active management as a standard on every real-money strategy, with targets that are real predictions and move with the trade; a promotion ladder that runs mechanically from a backtest pass to real money and back; more testing legs pushed through Stage 0; and longer and shorter timeframes, always net of cost.

slides.title: Roadmap 2 — machine learning and the desk
bullets: ML in the live loops — More learned decisions changing live orders, with serving and monitoring infrastructure.
Ten slots, one loop each — Every trade decision gets a question, a baseline, a label and a champion-versus-challenger test.
Regime and the desk — Learn when each strategy is primed; make the AI trading desk production-ready.
Data and labels — Grow the store of labelled outcomes, the binding constraint on every model.

slides.title: Roadmap 3 — the learning machine
bullets: Prop accounts — Automate, protect and qualify the prop-firm accounts.
Trustworthy plumbing — Every position protected, every close explained, every number labelled, every alert reaching the system without a human relaying it.
Research machine — Research programmes with weekly plans: questions run, get graded, and act.
Macro and value — A slower, thesis-driven sleeve expressed through defined-risk options.
slides.notes: The last part of the roadmap is about the machine that does the improving: prop accounts that qualify on their own, plumbing and alerts that can be trusted, research programmes that turn evidence into decisions without the operator in the path, and a slower macro and value sleeve. This is where the deck ends: no request, just the plan.

slides.title: Appendix A — system architecture
slides.notes: For technical readers. Five layers, kept separate on purpose. The runtime layer is the live trader: market data, strategy evaluation, order construction, per-account risk, broker execution, and a single trade journal database. The research layer holds backtests and ML training, on a separate machine. Operator communications, deployment and governance are their own layers. A web API feeds one dashboard.

rows: Market data · strategy evaluation · order build + validation · per-account risk · broker execution · trade journal
Backtest harnesses · ML datasets, training, registry · research queue runner
Request/response channel · alert and ping delivery
Service units · repo sync to the servers every few minutes · self-heal workflows
Canonical docs · work register · follow-through pipeline · CI guards

slides.title: Appendix B — what an evidence record contains
slides.notes: Each strategy has one evidence record, written by a script, never by hand. These are the fields that matter. Coverage state is read first, so a missing number is never mistaken for a bad one. Fidelity says whether the harness modelled every setting the live strategy uses.

rows: measured · harness_failed · no_harness · not_attempted — read first
Out-of-sample net R and R per trade, after the full cost stack
Sample size and how many separate time folds were positive
Fees, slippage allowance, funding allowance, with the source run
faithful = every configured lever modelled; approximate names the gaps
Rule id, when it was registered, and the verdict (pass / fail)
Max drawdown in R, worst trade, worst day — descriptive, not a verdict

slides.footnote: Source: comms/strategy_evidence/README.md and the records themselves (producer scripts/ops/build_strategy_evidence.py).

slides.notes: The same production legs with path detail: total net R over the test, and the largest peak-to-trough drawdown in R. Drawdown is descriptive here; it is not a pass mark. The ML model's record does not carry path statistics, shown as a dash.
